hints: Look closely at Fig. 4.1b where glycerol joins each fatty acid - focus on the -O- link next to the C=O group and recall the name for that -COO- linkage in lipids.
walkthrough:
See What Joins Glycerol to Fatty Acid**
In Fig. 4.1b each OH of glycerol has joined to the COOH of a fatty acid to give -O-C=O. That specific linkage between an alcohol and a carboxylic acid is always the same type of bond in lipids.

Name That Linkage**
That -COO- linkage is an ester bond. A triglyceride therefore contains three ester bonds, one for each fatty acid.

hints: Think about the general name for any reaction that joins two molecules together by removing -OH from one and -H from the other to release $H_2O$.
walkthrough:
Link Bond Formation to Water Release**
When the OH from glycerol and the OH from the fatty acid COOH combine, $H_2O$ is released and the ester bond is left behind. Joining with loss of water is the key clue.

Recall the Reaction Type**
Loss of water to build a larger molecule is a condensation reaction. The reverse, adding water to break it, would be hydrolysis.

hints: Compare the three zig-zag tails in Fig. 4.1a side by side - first check their overall length from top to bottom before looking at the details inside the chains.
Now look for kinks marked by double lines in the tails and recall how presence or absence of C=C double bonds defines saturated and unsaturated fatty acids.
Count exactly how many double-bond kinks each tail has to separate monounsaturated from polyunsaturated, and link this to X, Y and Z.
walkthrough:
Compare Chain Length**
Follow each hydrocarbon tail down. Y extends furthest, X is intermediate and Z is shortest. That means different numbers of carbon atoms, about 20 in Y, 18 in X and 16 in Z.

Check for Saturation**
A straight zig-zag with only single C-C bonds is saturated. A kink with a double line is a C=C double bond and makes the acid unsaturated. Z has no double lines so it is saturated, while X and Y both contain double lines so they are unsaturated.

Count Double Bonds**
X shows three double bonds so it is polyunsaturated. Y shows only one double bond so it is monounsaturated. Z shows zero double bonds, confirming it is fully saturated.

Final answer: hydrocarbon chains of different lengths - Y longest, Z shortest (X 18C, Y 20C, Z 16C); Z is saturated, X and Y are unsaturated; X is polyunsaturated with 3 C=C double bonds, Y is monounsaturated with 1 C=C double bond, Z has 0 C=C double bonds.

hints: Think about the chemistry of the three long fatty acid tails - what type of sharing of electrons occurs in C-C and C-H bonds and what does that mean for charge.
Now link that lack of charge to how the molecule behaves in water - can it dissolve and interact with polar water molecules.
walkthrough:
Why the Tails Are Non-polar**
The bulk of a triglyceride is three long hydrocarbon tails made of C-C and C-H bonds with equal sharing of electrons. There are no polar groups or charges there, so the tails are non-polar.

Result in Water**
Water is polar and interacts by hydrogen bonding. Non-polar tails cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, so triglycerides are insoluble and described as hydrophobic.
Final answer: fatty acid / hydrocarbon tails are non-polar with no charged groups; insoluble in water and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water.

hints: Recall what makes a membrane lipid special - think about the two opposite ends of a phospholipid and how each end behaves toward water.
Now compare a triglyceride to that pattern - does it have a water-attracting end, and what structure will it form in water instead of a flat bilayer.
walkthrough:
What a Membrane Needs**
Cell surface membranes need a bilayer with hydrophilic heads facing water outside and inside the cell and hydrophobic tails facing inward. In phospholipids the polar phosphate head provides that hydrophilic interaction with water by hydrogen bonding.

Why Triglycerides Fail**
Triglycerides are wholly hydrophobic with three fatty acids and no polar phosphate head. They cannot arrange head-to-water and tail-to-tail, so in water they clump as spheres, droplets or globules rather than a stable thin bilayer.

Final answer: triglycerides have no hydrophilic / polar phosphate head to interact with water; cannot form a bilayer and instead form droplets / micelles / globules, not a thin film, so not suitable for cell surface membranes.
